questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has taken oxycodone for chronic back pain for several months. Initially his pain was well controlled, but he now reports that the same dose no longer relieves it and he requires progressively higher amounts. Which of the following cellular changes best explains this loss of effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Upregulation of opioid receptors on target neurons

choices.label: B
choices.text: Desensitization and downregulation of opioid receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Irreversible mutation of the opioid receptor gene

choices.label: D
choices.text: Induction of hepatic CYP enzymes producing an inactive metabolite

choices.label: E
choices.text: Formation of neutralizing antibodies against oxycodone

explanation.summary: Tolerance reflects desensitization and downregulation of opioid receptors after chronic agonist exposure.
explanation.whyCorrect: With frequent opioid agonist use, opioid receptors become desensitized and downregulated, reducing signaling across all pathways so that higher doses are needed to produce the same effect. This tolerance can begin as early as two weeks of consistent use.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic agonist exposure downregulates rather than upregulates opioid receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tolerance is a reversible adaptive change, not an irreversible genetic mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick attributes tolerance to receptor changes, not to accelerated hepatic metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Opioids do not act by triggering neutralizing antibodies; tolerance is receptor-based.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman abruptly stops taking the opioids she has used daily for months. Within a day she develops tachycardia, hypertension, dilated pupils, shakiness, muscle pain, and severe anxiety. Activation of which of the following brainstem structures is most responsible for these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Locus coeruleus in the pons

choices.label: B
choices.text: Substantia nigra in the midbrain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nucleus accumbens

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ventral tegmental area

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus

explanation.summary: Opioid withdrawal is driven physiologically by activation of the locus coeruleus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Withdrawal is the body's response to abruptly stopping the drug. Its physiological basis is complex but involves activation of the locus coeruleus in the pons of the brainstem, a region normally involved in stress and panic responses, producing autonomic symptoms such as tachycardia, hypertension, and dilated pupils.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The substantia nigra governs motor control and dopamine in Parkinson disease, not opioid withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The nucleus accumbens participates in reward, but the brick names the locus coeruleus for withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The ventral tegmental area is a reward/dopamine center, not the driver of withdrawal symptoms here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The suprachiasmatic nucleus regulates circadian rhythm, not withdrawal physiology.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man is found unresponsive on the sidewalk. He has pinpoint pupils, a respiratory rate of 4/min with shallow breathing, and cyanotic lips. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate pharmacologic treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Naloxone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Buprenorphine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Methadone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Docusate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Flumazenil

explanation.summary: Naloxone is the reversal agent for opioid overdose.
explanation.whyCorrect: The findings are classic opioid overdose. Naloxone is a full opioid antagonist that binds and inhibits opioid receptors, displacing the agonist and reversing respiratory depression, which is the life-threatening feature here.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist used to ease withdrawal during discontinuation, not to reverse an acute overdose.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Methadone is a long-acting agonist for maintenance therapy and would worsen respiratory depression.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Docusate is a stool softener for opioid-induced constipation and has no role in overdose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with a heroin overdose is given naloxone in the emergency department and rapidly improves. About 45 minutes later she again becomes somnolent with slow, shallow breathing. Which of the following best explains this recurrence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Naloxone has a shorter duration of action than the opioid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Naloxone is a partial agonist that wears off into agonist activity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Naloxone caused rebound upregulation of opioid receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: The patient rapidly developed tolerance to naloxone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Naloxone accumulated in the liver and released the opioid

explanation.summary: Naloxone's duration of action is shorter than that of many opioids, so effects can return.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that the duration of action of the opioid antagonist is shorter than that of the agonists, so repeat doses of naloxone are often required in overdose situations. As naloxone wears off while opioid still occupies receptors, respiratory depression can recur.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Naloxone is a full antagonist, not a partial agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Recurrence is due to naloxone's short duration, not receptor upregulation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tolerance to naloxone over 45 minutes is not the mechanism described in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Naloxone does not sequester and later release the opioid from the liver.

questions.stem: A first responder administers a medication that competitively displaces an opioid already bound to its receptors and fully blocks all three opioid receptor types. Which of the following best describes this drug's mechanism of action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Full antagonism of all three opioid receptor types

choices.label: B
choices.text: Partial agonism at the mu opioid receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enhancement of GABA-mediated inhibition

choices.label: D
choices.text: Blockade of the benzodiazepine binding site

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibition of the CYP enzymes that metabolize the opioid

explanation.summary: Naloxone is a full opioid antagonist that binds all three receptor types.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike full or partial agonists, opioid antagonists fully bind and inhibit opioid receptors and can displace an agonist that is already bound. Naloxone, the classic example, antagonizes all three opioid receptor types and reverses respiratory depression.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Partial agonism describes buprenorphine, not the full antagonist being described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Opioid antagonists act at opioid receptors, not by enhancing GABA signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blocking the benzodiazepine site describes flumazenil, not an opioid antagonist.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The drug acts at the receptor, not by inhibiting hepatic metabolism of the opioid.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with opioid use disorder is about to be started on methadone for maintenance therapy. Which of the following studies should be obtained before initiating this medication, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An ECG, because methadone can prolong the QTc

choices.label: B
choices.text: Spirometry, because methadone causes bronchoconstriction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Liver function tests, because methadone is directly hepatotoxic

choices.label: D
choices.text: An MRI of the brain, because methadone raises intracranial pressure

choices.label: E
choices.text: A fasting glucose, because methadone causes hyperglycemia

explanation.summary: Methadone prolongs the QTc, so an ECG is obtained before starting it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Methadone influences cardiac muscle and can prolong the QTc, the interval between Q-wave polarization and T-wave repolarization. A prolonged QTc can lead to ventricular arrhythmias, so an ECG must be performed before a patient starts methadone.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Methadone's lethal cardiac effect is QTc prolongation, not bronchoconstriction detected by spirometry.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick highlights QTc prolongation as the reason for pre-treatment testing, not direct hepatotoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methadone is not associated with raised intracranial pressure requiring an MRI.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hyperglycemia is not the concern that prompts baseline testing before methadone.

questions.stem: A patient with an opioid overdose has progressively slow, shallow breathing that leads to a rising arterial pCO2 and eventual respiratory arrest. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the respiratory depression?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased brainstem chemoreceptor sensitivity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct paralysis of the diaphragm muscle fibers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bronchoconstriction that blocks airflow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pulmonary edema from acute fluid overload

choices.label: E
choices.text: A large increase in metabolic CO2 production

explanation.summary: Opioids reduce respiratory drive by lowering the brainstem's chemosensitivity to CO2.
explanation.whyCorrect: Opioids reduce respiratory drive by binding mu receptors. Their inhibitory effects decrease the brain's chemosensitivity to high blood pCO2 and to hypoxia, so breathing slows and becomes shallow; ventilation falls, arterial pCO2 rises, and the result can be unconsciousness, respiratory arrest, and death.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Opioids depress the central respiratory drive rather than directly paralyzing diaphragm fibers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The mechanism is reduced central drive, not airway bronchoconstriction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Respiratory failure here is from hypoventilation, not fluid-overload pulmonary edema.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The problem is decreased ventilation, not increased CO2 production.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman is being started on a scheduled opioid for chronic pain. To prevent a common and predictable adverse effect, which of the following is most appropriate to prescribe alongside the opioid?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A stool softener

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loperamide

choices.label: C
choices.text: A scheduled antiemetic only

choices.label: D
choices.text: An increased opioid dose

choices.label: E
choices.text: Scheduled naloxone

explanation.summary: Opioid-induced constipation is anticipated and prevented with a stool softener or laxative.
explanation.whyCorrect: Opioids reduce bowel motility, and opioid-induced constipation is a common, concerning adverse effect. It is common practice to prescribe a stool softener such as docusate, or a laxative, even before the patient has symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Loperamide is an antidiarrheal that slows the gut further and would worsen constipation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An antiemetic may help nausea but does not address the predictable constipation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Raising the opioid dose worsens, rather than prevents, gastrointestinal adverse effects.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Naloxone reverses overdose and would precipitate withdrawal, not prevent constipation.

questions.stem: A physician is distinguishing dependence from addiction in a patient on chronic opioids. Which of the following statements best describes addiction as defined in the brick?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Compulsive drug seeking and use despite harmful consequences

choices.label: B
choices.text: Needing progressively higher doses to achieve the same effect

choices.label: C
choices.text: A physiologic adaptation requiring the drug to feel normal at baseline

choices.label: D
choices.text: Autonomic symptoms that appear after abruptly stopping the drug

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reversal of the drug's effect when an antagonist is administered

explanation.summary: Addiction is a chronic relapsing brain disease of compulsive use despite harm.
explanation.whyCorrect: Per the National Institute on Drug Abuse definition cited in the brick, addiction is a chronic, relapsing brain disease characterized by compulsive drug seeking and use despite harmful consequences. This is distinct from dependence, which is a physiologic adaptation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Needing higher doses for the same effect describes tolerance, not addiction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Requiring the drug to function at baseline describes dependence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Autonomic symptoms after abrupt cessation describe withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reversal of effect by an antagonist describes the action of naloxone, not addiction.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man on long-term opioids for chronic pain wishes to discontinue them while minimizing severe withdrawal. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacologic strategy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Transition to buprenorphine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Administer scheduled naloxone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stop the opioid abruptly today

choices.label: D
choices.text: Double the opioid dose and then stop

choices.label: E
choices.text: Start flumazenil

explanation.summary: A partial agonist such as buprenorphine helps mitigate withdrawal during discontinuation.
explanation.whyCorrect: To limit withdrawal symptoms in patients discontinuing opioids, a tapering strategy or the partial agonist buprenorphine may be used. Buprenorphine partially activates opioid receptors, blunting withdrawal as the patient comes off opioids.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Naloxone is a full antagonist that would precipitate acute withdrawal in a dependent patient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Abrupt cessation produces the severe withdrawal the plan is meant to avoid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increasing the dose worsens dependence rather than easing discontinuation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and has no role in opioid discontinuation.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man who injects heroin presents with fever, a new heart murmur, and blood cultures positive for bacteria. This complication is most directly related to which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sharing of needles

choices.label: B
choices.text: Methadone-induced QTc prolongation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Acute opioid withdrawal

choices.label: D
choices.text: Opioid-induced constipation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Development of tolerance to heroin

explanation.summary: Needle sharing during IV opioid use causes bloodborne infections such as endocarditis and sepsis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Secondary adverse effects from opioid abuse include infections when opioids are used intravenously outside the medical system. Needle sharing exposes users to bacterial, viral, and fungal infections and can cause heart valve infections or systemic bacterial infection (sepsis), which can be fatal.

whyWrongByChoice.B: QTc prolongation is a methadone cardiac effect, not a cause of infective endocarditis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Withdrawal produces autonomic symptoms, not a bacteremic valvular infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Constipation is a gastrointestinal effect unrelated to endocarditis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tolerance is a receptor adaptation and does not cause bloodborne infection.

questions.stem: An opioid-dependent patient is given naloxone in the emergency department. Minutes later he becomes agitated and diaphoretic with tachycardia and dilated pupils. Which of the following best explains this reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Naloxone precipitated acute opioid withdrawal

choices.label: B
choices.text: An anaphylactic allergic reaction to naloxone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Worsening of the opioid overdose

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serotonin syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Methadone toxicity

explanation.summary: Because naloxone blocks all opioid receptors, it can precipitate immediate withdrawal.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that because naloxone antagonizes all opioid receptors after administration, it can cause immediate withdrawal, and patients may be violent and agitated following its use. The agitation, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and dilated pupils are classic withdrawal findings.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The signs are the autonomic picture of withdrawal, not urticaria and airway compromise of anaphylaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Naloxone reverses opioid effects; it does not deepen the overdose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: There is no serotonergic agent described, and the picture matches opioid withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The patient received naloxone, not methadone, and shows withdrawal rather than sedation.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has taken a scheduled opioid for chronic hip pain for 6 months. She takes it exactly as prescribed, has never sought early refills, and has no cravings. She reports that on the two occasions she forgot a dose she felt unwell and could not go about her day until she took it. Which of the following terms best describes her condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Addiction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tolerance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Opioid use disorder

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dependence

choices.label: E
choices.text: Opioid overdose

explanation.summary: Dependence is the state in which the body has adapted to a drug and needs it to function at baseline.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dependence is what happens when the body has adapted to a drug and the patient needs the drug to function at their baseline or normal state. Her inability to function normally when a dose is missed, without any compulsive use or craving, is dependence, which is a physiologic adaptation and does not usually lead to addiction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Addiction requires compulsive drug seeking and use despite harmful consequences, which she does not show.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Tolerance is a loss of drug effect requiring higher doses; her doses are stable and effective.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Opioid use disorder requires DSM-5 criteria such as craving or hazardous use, which are absent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Overdose presents with respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils, not a missed-dose feeling of being unwell.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man taking daily opioids for chronic low back pain suddenly runs out of his medication. Two days later he reports that his back pain is far worse than it was before he ever started opioids, and even light touch to the area is painful. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Desensitization of opioid receptors from continued agonist binding

choices.label: B
choices.text: Upregulation of opioid receptors after abrupt removal of the agonist

choices.label: C
choices.text: Induction of hepatic CYP enzymes by chronic opioid exposure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progression of the underlying spinal disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Blunted brainstem chemosensitivity to carbon dioxide

explanation.summary: Abrupt withdrawal of an opioid from a dependent patient allows the compensated, downregulated receptors to upregulate, producing the opposite effect, such as hyperalgesia.
explanation.whyCorrect: With frequent opioid use, receptors become desensitized or downregulated, and the body compensates for this downregulation. If the drug is abruptly taken away, receptors can be upregulated, causing an opposite effect; a patient taking daily opioids for chronic pain who suddenly runs out of medication can experience hyperalgesia as a result.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Desensitization occurs while the agonist is present and underlies tolerance, not the rebound after the drug is removed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The hyperalgesia is a receptor-level rebound, not a change in hepatic metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The abrupt timing after running out of medication points to withdrawal-related hyperalgesia rather than disease progression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blunted chemosensitivity explains opioid respiratory depression, not increased pain after cessation.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman is prescribed oxycodone after surgery and continues to take it consistently every day. Her physician warns her that the medication may begin to lose effectiveness at the same dose. Tolerance to opioids can develop as early as which of the following intervals of consistent use?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Two days

choices.label: B
choices.text: One week

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two weeks

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two months

choices.label: E
choices.text: Six months

explanation.summary: Opioid tolerance can occur as early as two weeks following consistent use.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tolerance results from desensitization and downregulation of opioid receptors with frequent agonist use, so that increasing doses are required to produce a similar effect. It can occur as early as two weeks following consistent use of opioids.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Two days of use is too short for the receptor downregulation that underlies tolerance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The threshold given for earliest tolerance is two weeks, not one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tolerance can appear well before two months of consistent use.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tolerance does not require six months; it can develop within weeks.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man stops using opioids after several months of daily use. In addition to physical signs, he develops a set of psychological withdrawal symptoms. Which of the following is best classified as a psychological, rather than physical, symptom of opioid withdrawal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Insomnia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tachycardia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dilated pupils

choices.label: D
choices.text: Muscle pain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hypertension

explanation.summary: Opioid withdrawal has both physical and psychological components; insomnia is among the psychological symptoms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Withdrawal can be physical and psychological. Physical symptoms include tachycardia, hypertension, dilated pupils, shakiness, and muscle pain, whereas psychological symptoms include anxiety, agitation, insomnia, mood changes, or depression.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Tachycardia is a physical (autonomic) symptom of withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dilated pupils are a physical sign of withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Muscle pain is listed among the physical symptoms of withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypertension is a physical autonomic symptom of withdrawal.

questions.stem: A physician counsels a 44-year-old woman about the risks of a long-term opioid prescription for chronic pain. She asks what proportion of patients prescribed opioids go on to develop clinical opioid use disorder. Which of the following is the most accurate estimate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Less than 1%

explanation.summary: About 8-12% of patients prescribed opioids may develop clinical opioid use disorder.
explanation.whyCorrect: Between 20-30% of patients prescribed opioids for chronic pain misuse the medication as a result of dependence and addiction, and 8-12% of patients prescribed opioids may develop clinical opioid use disorder. These statistics motivate prescribing the shortest duration and minimum amount needed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The risk is substantially higher than 1%, which is why opioid stewardship matters.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The cited rate of clinical opioid use disorder is 8-12%, not 2-4%.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 20-30% is the proportion of chronic-pain patients who misuse the medication, not the rate of clinical opioid use disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 40-50% overstates the rate of opioid use disorder among prescribed patients.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man prescribed oxycodone for a shoulder injury reports strong cravings for the drug, has repeatedly operated heavy machinery while intoxicated, and takes his wife's hydrocodone when his own supply runs out so that he will not feel sick. Which of the following best characterizes these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Criteria for opioid use disorder as defined in the DSM-5

choices.label: B
choices.text: Physiologic dependence without any behavioral component

choices.label: C
choices.text: Expected non-lethal adverse effects of opioid therapy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tolerance from downregulation of opioid receptors alone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Acute opioid withdrawal driven by the locus coeruleus

explanation.summary: Craving, use in physically hazardous situations, and using a similar substance to avoid withdrawal are DSM-5 criteria for opioid use disorder.
explanation.whyCorrect: Criteria for opioid use disorder are found in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition. Symptoms include craving or strong desire, recurrent use in situations that are physically hazardous, tolerance, withdrawal symptoms, and using a drug or similar substance to relieve or avoid withdrawal symptoms; this patient shows several of these.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Craving and hazardous use are behavioral features that go beyond simple physiologic dependence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Non-lethal adverse effects are constipation, nausea, sedation, and dizziness, not craving and hazardous use.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tolerance alone would not explain craving or using another person's medication in hazardous circumstances.
whyWrongByChoice.E: He is avoiding withdrawal by taking a similar drug; his presentation is not an acute withdrawal state.

questions.stem: Two patients receive opioid analgesia after surgery: one receives fentanyl and the other receives hydrocodone. The anesthesiologist notes that the fentanyl patient must be monitored especially closely for adverse effects. Which of the following properties of fentanyl best explains this heightened concern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Its ultra-long half-life

choices.label: B
choices.text: Its very high potency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Its partial agonist activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its tendency to prolong the QTc

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its lack of hepatic metabolism

explanation.summary: Fentanyl's high potency gives it a higher potential for adverse effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adverse effects of opioids range from tolerable to lethal depending on the drug and the dose. Potency differs between opioids; fentanyl, a very potent opioid, has a higher potential for adverse effects because of its high potency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An ultra-long half-life is the property attributed to methadone, not fentanyl.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Buprenorphine is the partial agonist discussed; fentanyl's risk relates to potency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: QTc prolongation is the cardiac concern with methadone, not the reason fentanyl is dangerous.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Many opioids are hepatically metabolized by the CYP system; lack of metabolism is not the issue.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman experiences profound sedation and slowed breathing after a standard dose of an oral opioid that most patients tolerate well. Genetic testing later reveals a polymorphism in a hepatic enzyme. Which of the following best explains her exaggerated response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Upregulation of opioid receptors from prior abstinence

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased renal excretion of the parent opioid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Altered hepatic CYP metabolism changing the drug level

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced gastric motility delaying drug absorption

choices.label: E
choices.text: Activation of the locus coeruleus in the pons

explanation.summary: Drug levels, and therefore adverse effects, depend on CYP metabolism, and genetic polymorphisms in this system can contribute to toxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: In addition to how much drug a patient takes, drug levels are affected by how the drug is metabolized. Many opioids are hepatically metabolized by the CYP system, and alterations to this system, such as genetic polymorphisms, can contribute to adverse effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Receptor upregulation follows abrupt withdrawal in a dependent patient and produces opposite effects, not an exaggerated response to a first dose.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Increased renal excretion would lower, not raise, drug exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reduced gastric motility is an opioid adverse effect, not a genetic cause of altered drug levels.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Locus coeruleus activation underlies withdrawal, not excess sedation and respiratory depression.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man started a scheduled opioid for cancer-related pain 3 days ago. He reports that the medication controls his pain well but he feels sleepy and dizzy. His breathing and vital signs are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate counseling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: These effects are expected to lessen as he adjusts to the dose

choices.label: B
choices.text: These effects indicate early overdose and he should take naloxone

choices.label: C
choices.text: These effects mean tolerance has developed and the dose must rise

choices.label: D
choices.text: These effects signal withdrawal and he should take an extra dose

choices.label: E
choices.text: These effects will persist unchanged for the duration of therapy

explanation.summary: Sedation and dizziness from opioids are mitigated as the patient becomes adjusted to the dose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the most common non-lethal side effects of opioids are constipation, nausea, sedation, and dizziness. Some of these adverse effects, such as sedation and dizziness, will be mitigated as the patient becomes adjusted to the dose.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Overdose involves severe respiratory depression, pinpoint pupils, and unresponsiveness; his breathing and vitals are normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tolerance is loss of pain relief requiring higher doses; his pain is well controlled.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Withdrawal follows stopping the drug and presents with tachycardia, hypertension, and dilated pupils, not sedation on a new drug.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sedation and dizziness typically diminish with adjustment rather than persisting unchanged.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman develops persistent nausea and occasional vomiting after starting an oral opioid for postoperative pain. Which of the following mechanisms best explains these symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blunted brainstem chemosensitivity to carbon dioxide

choices.label: B
choices.text: Activation of the locus coeruleus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Downregulation of opioid receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prolongation of ventricular repolarization

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduction in gastric motility

explanation.summary: Opioids reduce bowel and gastric motility, which leads to constipation and induces nausea or vomiting.
explanation.whyCorrect: Opioids reduce bowel motility. Reduction in gastric motility may lead to constipation and induce feelings of nausea or vomiting, making these among the most common non-lethal adverse effects.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blunted CO2 chemosensitivity explains respiratory depression, not nausea.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Locus coeruleus activation underlies withdrawal symptoms, not nausea from an ongoing opioid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Receptor downregulation explains tolerance, not the gastrointestinal effects.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prolonged repolarization (QTc) is a cardiac effect of methadone, unrelated to nausea.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man on a stable dose of oxycodone for chronic pain is seen for a routine visit. He is alert and conversant, with a respiratory rate of 16/min and normal blood pressure. Examination shows pinpoint pupils bilaterally. Which of the following best explains the pupillary finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Opioid overdose requiring immediate naloxone reversal

choices.label: B
choices.text: Early opioid withdrawal from a missed dose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Methadone-related cardiac toxicity with QT prolongation

choices.label: D
choices.text: An expected non-lethal adverse effect of the opioid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Development of tolerance to the analgesic effect of the opioid

explanation.summary: Miosis (pinpoint pupils) from pupillary constriction is a non-lethal adverse effect of opioids and does not by itself indicate overdose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Miosis (pinpoint pupils) due to pupillary constriction may occur among the non-lethal adverse effects of opioids. In an alert patient with a normal respiratory rate and blood pressure, the pinpoint pupils reflect this expected effect rather than overdose.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Overdose presents with slow, irregular, or stopped breathing, unresponsiveness, and bradycardia; he is alert with normal breathing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Withdrawal produces dilated pupils, not pinpoint pupils.
whyWrongByChoice.C: He is not on methadone, and QTc prolongation does not affect pupil size.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tolerance is a loss of drug effect requiring higher doses; it does not cause miosis.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student is asked to name the adverse effects of opioids that most commonly cause death. Which of the following pairs is the best answer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Constipation and nausea with protracted vomiting

choices.label: B
choices.text: Respiratory arrest and cardiac arrhythmias

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sedation and dizziness with falls

choices.label: D
choices.text: Miosis and opioid-induced hyperalgesia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Insomnia and anxiety with agitation

explanation.summary: The most common lethal side effects of opioids are respiratory arrest and cardiac arrhythmias.
explanation.whyCorrect: Opioid adverse effects range from tolerable to lethal. The most common lethal side effects are respiratory arrest, from reduced respiratory drive, and cardiac arrhythmias, such as those following QTc prolongation with methadone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Constipation and nausea are among the most common non-lethal side effects.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sedation and dizziness are non-lethal effects that diminish as the patient adjusts to the dose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Miosis is a non-lethal effect and hyperalgesia is a withdrawal phenomenon; neither is a primary cause of death.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Insomnia and anxiety are psychological withdrawal symptoms, not lethal adverse effects.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department somnolent after taking a large dose of an opioid. His respiratory rate is 6/min with shallow breaths. Which of the following changes is most likely to be present on arterial blood gas analysis, and why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated arterial pCO2, because ventilation has dropped

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased arterial pCO2, because hypoxia triggers hyperventilation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Normal arterial pCO2, because chemoreceptors compensate fully

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decreased arterial pCO2, because respiratory muscle strength increases

choices.label: E
choices.text: Elevated arterial pO2, because breathing is slow but deep

explanation.summary: In opioid overdose, breathing slows and becomes shallow, ventilation drops, and arterial pCO2 rises.
explanation.whyCorrect: Opioids reduce respiratory drive via mu receptors, blunt the brain's chemosensitivity to high pCO2 and hypoxia, and reduce the strength and central drive to respiratory muscles. The net result is that breathing slows and becomes shallower, ventilation drops, and arterial pCO2 rises, leading to somnolence and, eventually, respiratory arrest.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypoxia would normally cause hyperventilation, but this response is lessened when opioids are present.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chemoreceptor responses are blunted by opioids, so pCO2 does not stay normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Opioids reduce, not increase, the strength and central drive to respiratory muscles.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Breathing is slow and shallow, so oxygenation falls rather than rises.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man on methadone maintenance therapy has an episode of syncope. An ECG obtained afterward shows a markedly prolonged QTc. Which of the following complications is he at greatest risk for?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete heart block

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pulmonary embolism

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ventricular arrhythmia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Infective endocarditis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Acute respiratory arrest

explanation.summary: A prolonged QTc from methadone can lead to ventricular arrhythmias.
explanation.whyCorrect: Certain opioids, such as methadone, influence the cardiac muscle and may prolong QTc. Having a prolonged QTc can lead to ventricular arrhythmias, which is why an ECG must be performed before a patient starts methadone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The QTc-related danger described is ventricular arrhythmia, not conduction block.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pulmonary embolism is unrelated to QTc prolongation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Endocarditis is a complication of needle sharing, not of a prolonged QTc.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Respiratory arrest is an opioid overdose effect, not the consequence of QTc prolongation.

questions.stem: Before starting a patient on methadone, a physician measures the QTc on the pre-treatment ECG. The QTc represents the length of time between which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Onset of the P wave and onset of the QRS complex

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two consecutive R waves

choices.label: C
choices.text: Onset and end of the QRS complex

choices.label: D
choices.text: End of the T wave and the next P wave

choices.label: E
choices.text: Q-wave polarization and T-wave repolarization

explanation.summary: QTc measures the interval from Q-wave polarization to T-wave repolarization.
explanation.whyCorrect: QTc is a measure on an electrocardiogram of the length between Q-wave polarization and T-wave repolarization. Methadone can prolong this interval, which can lead to ventricular arrhythmias.

whyWrongByChoice.A: P-wave onset to QRS onset is the PR interval, not the QTc.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The R-R interval reflects heart rate, not the QTc.
whyWrongByChoice.C: QRS onset to end is the QRS duration, not the QTc.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The interval from T wave to the next P wave is not the QTc.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man with opioid use disorder is transitioned from heroin to methadone. He notes that when he misses methadone doses, his withdrawal symptoms are much milder than those he experienced when he ran out of heroin. Which of the following properties of methadone best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Partial agonism at opioid receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ultra-long half-life

choices.label: C
choices.text: Full antagonism at opioid receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Very high potency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lack of CYP-mediated metabolism

explanation.summary: Methadone produces much less severe withdrawal because of its ultra-long half-life.
explanation.whyCorrect: To limit opioid withdrawal in patients discontinuing opioids, options include a tapering strategy, the partial agonist buprenorphine, or methadone, which has much less severe withdrawal symptoms due to the ultra-long half-life of the medication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Partial agonism describes buprenorphine; methadone is an opioid agonist used for maintenance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Full antagonism describes naloxone, which precipitates rather than blunts withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Very high potency is the property attributed to fentanyl and raises adverse-effect risk; it does not soften withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metabolism is not the explanation given; the milder withdrawal reflects methadone's ultra-long half-life.

questions.stem: A bystander is taught to recognize opioid overdose so that naloxone can be given promptly. Which of the following findings is a sign of opioid overdose rather than withdrawal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tachycardia with a racing heartbeat

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dilated pupils with tearing eyes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypertension with a flushed face

choices.label: D
choices.text: Blue or purple fingernails and lips

choices.label: E
choices.text: Shakiness with sweating and goosebumps

explanation.summary: Blue or purple fingernails and lips are a sign of opioid overdose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Signs and symptoms of opioid overdose include slow, irregular, or stopped breathing, pinpoint pupils, unresponsiveness, bradycardia or low blood pressure, blue or purple fingernails and lips, and pale or clammy skin. Cyanotic nails and lips reflect the hypoventilation of overdose.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tachycardia is a sign of withdrawal; overdose causes bradycardia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dilated pupils occur in withdrawal; overdose causes pinpoint pupils.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypertension is a withdrawal sign; overdose produces low blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shakiness is a physical symptom of withdrawal, not overdose.

questions.stem: Heroin is bound to opioid receptors in a patient with respiratory depression. Naloxone is administered and displaces the heroin from those receptors within minutes, restoring breathing. Which of the following properties of naloxone allows it to displace an agonist that is already bound?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Irreversible covalent binding to the receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: A longer duration of action than the agonist

choices.label: C
choices.text: Partial intrinsic activity at the receptor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of the hepatic metabolism of the agonist

choices.label: E
choices.text: A higher affinity for the opioid receptor than the agonist

explanation.summary: Naloxone has a higher affinity for the opioid receptor, so it displaces a bound agonist and reverses its effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: If an opioid receptor is already bound by an agonist, an opioid antagonist can displace the agonist and reverse the effects. When an antagonist such as naloxone is given, it has a higher affinity for the opiate receptor, and as a result it displaces the agonist and antagonizes all three receptor types, reversing respiratory depression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Naloxone binds competitively and reversibly; its effects wear off, which is why repeat doses are often needed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Naloxone's duration of action is shorter than that of the agonists, not longer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Naloxone is a full antagonist with no agonist activity; partial intrinsic activity describes buprenorphine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Naloxone acts at the receptor, not by altering hepatic metabolism of the opioid.

questions.stem: The mother of a 22-year-old man with opioid use disorder asks a pharmacist how she can obtain naloxone to keep at home in case of an overdose. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is now widely available over the counter in many states

choices.label: B
choices.text: It can only be dispensed after a screening ECG

choices.label: C
choices.text: It may only be administered in a hospital setting

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is restricted to licensed first responders

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires enrollment in a methadone program

explanation.summary: Naloxone is carried by all first responders and is now widely available over the counter in many states.
explanation.whyCorrect: Naloxone is a life-saving opioid antagonist that is carried by all first responders and is now widely available over the counter in many states across the country, allowing bystanders and family members to reverse an overdose.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A screening ECG is required before starting methadone, not before obtaining naloxone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Naloxone is designed for use outside the hospital, including by first responders and the public.
whyWrongByChoice.D: First responders carry it, but its availability is not restricted to them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Naloxone access is not tied to methadone maintenance enrollment.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man has just undergone a difficult extraction of four wisdom teeth, two of which were impacted. He is expected to have significant pain for the next day or two. His mother is worried he will become "hooked." Which of the following is the most appropriate prescribing approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 30-day supply of hydrocodone to avoid the need for refills

choices.label: B
choices.text: Around-the-clock hydrocodone scheduled for the next two weeks

choices.label: C
choices.text: A small quantity of hydrocodone plus a non-narcotic analgesic

choices.label: D
choices.text: An extended-release opioid formulation taken once daily

choices.label: E
choices.text: Methadone in place of a short-acting opioid for the pain

explanation.summary: Good opioid stewardship means prescribing the minimum amount for the shortest duration, alongside a non-narcotic medicine, and stopping the opioid as soon as pain lessens.
explanation.whyCorrect: To avoid dependence and addiction, it is important to use the lowest dose for the shortest amount of time needed to treat the pain. In the case, the prescription is limited to just 12 pills to get through the painful time, a non-narcotic medicine is started for additional relief, ice is used, and the patient is told to stop the hydrocodone as soon as he has less pain and not to take it if he does not need it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A 30-day supply far exceeds the minimum amount needed for a day or two of pain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Scheduled dosing for two weeks prolongs exposure; tolerance can begin within two weeks of consistent use.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An extended-release opioid extends exposure rather than minimizing it for brief acute pain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Methadone is used for maintenance therapy and requires a baseline ECG; it is not the choice for brief postoperative pain.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman has taken a stable dose of a prescribed opioid for chronic pain for 1 year. Her daughter is alarmed that her mother feels ill when a dose is missed and asks whether this means her mother is "addicted." Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Feeling ill when a dose is missed confirms addiction

choices.label: B
choices.text: The opioid should be stopped immediately to prevent addiction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Naloxone should be given to test for addiction

choices.label: D
choices.text: This is dependence, which does not usually lead to addiction

choices.label: E
choices.text: This is tolerance, which is the same thing as addiction

explanation.summary: Dependence is a physiologic adaptation that does not usually lead to addiction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients who take opioids can become tolerant and develop dependence and addiction, but dependence does not usually lead to addiction. Feeling unwell when a dose is missed reflects dependence, a physiologic adaptation, whereas addiction is a compulsion to seek and use the drug despite harm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Missed-dose symptoms reflect dependence and withdrawal, not compulsive use despite harm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Abrupt cessation in a dependent patient precipitates withdrawal; tapering is used instead.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Naloxone would precipitate withdrawal in a dependent patient and is not a diagnostic test for addiction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tolerance is loss of drug effect at a given dose and is distinct from addiction.

questions.stem: A medical student asks why opioids, unlike many other drug classes, so readily predispose patients to tolerance, dependence, withdrawal, and addiction. Which of the following best explains this predisposition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: High concentration of opioid receptors throughout the CNS acting on pain, sedation, and reward pathways

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exclusive distribution of opioid receptors in the peripheral nervous system and gut

choices.label: C
choices.text: Irreversible covalent binding of opioids to their receptors in the spinal cord

choices.label: D
choices.text: Absence of hepatic metabolism, causing opioids to accumulate in the CNS

choices.label: E
choices.text: Direct enhancement of GABA-mediated inhibition in the pons and brainstem

explanation.summary: Opioids predispose to tolerance, dependence, withdrawal, and addiction because of the high concentration of opioid receptors throughout the CNS and their impact on pain, sedation, and reward pathways.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike many drugs, opioids may predispose patients to tolerance, dependence, withdrawal, and/or addiction. This is related to the high concentration of opioid receptors throughout the CNS and their impact on pain, sedation, reward, and many other pathways.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Opioid receptors are widely distributed throughout the CNS, which is precisely why these phenomena occur.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Opioid binding is reversible; naloxone can displace bound agonists.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Many opioids are hepatically metabolized by the CYP system.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Opioids act at opioid receptors, not by enhancing GABA-mediated inhibition.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman has taken a moderate dose of oxycodone daily for 3 months after a fracture. Her pain has resolved and she wishes to stop the medication. Her withdrawal risk is judged to be mild. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial strategy to avoid withdrawal symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Stop the oxycodone abruptly

choices.label: B
choices.text: Slowly decrease the oxycodone dose over time

choices.label: C
choices.text: Give a single dose of naloxone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Switch to fentanyl and then stop

choices.label: E
choices.text: Add docusate and continue the same dose

explanation.summary: Withdrawal can be avoided by tapering, that is, slowly decreasing the drug dose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dependence and withdrawal result from abrupt removal of the drug in a patient whose receptors have been downregulated. Withdrawal can be avoided by tapering (slowly decreasing the drug dose), or, in more severe cases, with the use of drugs like buprenorphine or methadone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Abrupt cessation in a dependent patient produces withdrawal symptoms and even hyperalgesia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Naloxone is a full antagonist that precipitates immediate withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Switching to a very potent opioid does not address discontinuation and raises adverse-effect risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Docusate prevents opioid-induced constipation; it does nothing to ease discontinuation.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man has used opioids daily for 2 years and has developed marked tolerance, requiring several times his original dose for pain relief. His receptors have become desensitized and downregulated. Which of the following best describes the effect of this downregulation on opioid signaling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only the pain pathway loses signaling, sparing sedation and reward

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only the reward pathway loses signaling, sparing pain and respiration

choices.label: C
choices.text: Signaling is reduced across pain, sedation, respiratory, and reward pathways

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only the respiratory pathway loses signaling, sparing pain and reward

choices.label: E
choices.text: Signaling is increased across all pathways to compensate for the drug

explanation.summary: Receptor downregulation in tolerance reduces signaling outputs on all opioid pathways: pain, sedation, respiratory, and reward.
explanation.whyCorrect: Over time, opioid receptors can be desensitized or downregulated as a result of frequent opioid agonist use. This downregulation of the receptors reduces signaling outputs on all pathways, namely pain, sedation, respiratory, and reward pathways, which is why the patient needs escalating doses for a similar effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The downregulation is not selective for the pain pathway; sedation, respiratory, and reward signaling fall as well.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reward is one of several pathways affected, not the only one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Respiratory signaling falls along with pain, sedation, and reward; it is not selectively affected.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Downregulation reduces rather than increases signaling; upregulation occurs only after the drug is abruptly removed.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is started on an opioid for severe postoperative pain. His physician explains that although the drug binds several opioid receptor subtypes, most of its pain-relieving effect comes from activation of one particular receptor. Activation of which of the following receptors is responsible for the majority of an opioid's analgesic effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Delta-opioid receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kappa-opioid receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mu-opioid receptor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sigma receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Omega receptor

explanation.summary: Most of the analgesic properties of opioids are mediated by the mu-opioid receptor.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that most of the analgesic properties of opioids are due to activation of the mu-opioid receptor, including activation in the periaqueductal gray that blocks the sensation of pain. Mu, kappa, and delta are the three receptors involved in analgesia, but the mu receptor carries the bulk of the effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Delta-opioid receptors contribute to analgesia and modulate mu activity but are found in the fewest brain areas and mainly produce antidepressant/anxiolytic effects.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Kappa-opioid receptors provide and modulate analgesia but are not targeted for long-term analgesia because they cause dysphoria and depression.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sigma is not one of the three primary opioid receptors (mu, kappa, delta) involved in analgesia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Omega is not an opioid receptor type.

questions.stem: A pharmacology instructor compares two opioids that both bind the mu-opioid receptor with high affinity. She notes that the full agonist produces a wider array of signaling cascades and a greater maximal physiologic effect than the partial agonist. The full agonist differs from the partial agonist primarily by having a higher which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absorption

choices.label: B
choices.text: Duration of action

choices.label: C
choices.text: Efficacy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Renal excretion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Receptor affinity

explanation.summary: A full agonist has ~100% efficacy at the receptor, whereas a partial agonist has lower efficacy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that full agonists completely bind receptors and produce the full array of physiologic effects, giving them higher efficacy than partial agonists. A full agonist has 100% efficacy when binding to a receptor, whereas a partial agonist produces a lesser (partial) effect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Absorption is a pharmacokinetic property that is not what distinguishes full from partial agonists.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Duration reflects how long the drug remains bound and acts, and is independent of full versus partial agonism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Excretion is a pharmacokinetic property and is not the defining difference.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both full and partial agonists bind with high affinity; the difference lies in efficacy, not affinity.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with acute severe pain from a long-bone fracture. The team wants an opioid route that avoids first-pass metabolism and provides the quickest onset of analgesia. Which of the following routes of administration best meets these goals?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oral

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intramuscular

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intravenous

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transdermal

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rectal

explanation.summary: The intravenous route avoids first-pass metabolism and gives the fastest onset, making it preferred for acute severe pain.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies IV as the preferred route for acute severe pain because it provides a quicker onset of action, avoids first-pass metabolism, and most often yields higher bioavailability than the oral route.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oral opioids are subject to first-pass metabolism and have a slower onset and potentially lower bioavailability.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IM avoids first-pass metabolism but has a slower onset than IV and is the least common route for opioids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Transdermal delivery is slow-absorbing and used for chronic/sustained pain, not rapid onset.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The rectal route is not described as the preferred rapid-onset route for acute severe pain.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man of Asian descent is given a standard analgesic dose of an opioid after surgery. He becomes excessively sedated and develops respiratory depression, and the effect of a single dose lasts far longer than expected. A CYP2D6 phenotype is suspected. Which of the following best explains this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is a poor metabolizer, so clearance is slowed

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is an ultrarapid metabolizer, so the opioid is cleared very quickly

choices.label: C
choices.text: He has induced CYP2D6 activity, lowering opioid levels

choices.label: D
choices.text: He lacks opioid receptors, increasing free drug in plasma

choices.label: E
choices.text: He has enhanced renal clearance shortening the drug's half-life

explanation.summary: Poor CYP2D6 metabolizers clear opioids slowly, prolonging drug action and risking overdose; this phenotype is most common in individuals of Asian descent (up to 35%).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that poor metabolizers have altered pharmacokinetics that prolong the duration of action, so a single dose can last two to three times as long as expected and cause unintended overdose. Poor metabolizers are most common among individuals of Asian descent (up to 35%).

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ultrarapid metabolizers clear drug quickly and have shorter, not prolonged, durations of action.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Induced CYP2D6 would lower opioid levels and reduce effect, the opposite of this prolonged toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Opioid receptor number is not the mechanism of altered duration described in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick attributes altered opioid duration to CYP2D6 hepatic metabolism, not to enhanced renal clearance.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with opioid use disorder is started on a medication to help manage his condition. His physician selects a drug that binds the mu-opioid receptor with high affinity but only partially activates it, so that at high doses the patient gets less of a 'high.' Which of the following medications was most likely prescribed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Buprenorphine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Morphine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fentanyl

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hydromorphone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Codeine

explanation.summary: Buprenorphine is the most common partial mu-opioid agonist and is used in opioid use disorder.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes buprenorphine as the most common partial agonist of the mu-opioid receptor. It binds with high affinity but only partially activates the receptor, so at high doses patients get less of a 'high,' making it useful in opioid use disorder.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Morphine is a strong full agonist used as the potency benchmark, not a partial agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fentanyl is a strong full agonist and would not blunt the 'high' as described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydromorphone is a strong full agonist, not a partial agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Codeine is a weak full agonist (and prodrug), not a partial agonist.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is given codeine for pain after a tonsillectomy. Hours later he develops profound respiratory depression. Genetic testing reveals a CYP2D6 polymorphism. Which of the following mechanisms best explains his toxicity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolism converts codeine to morphine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Poor CYP2D6 metabolism prevents codeine from being activated at all

choices.label: C
choices.text: Codeine directly antagonizes brainstem mu receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced renal excretion accumulates unchanged codeine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Codeine induces its own metabolism, raising active metabolite levels

explanation.summary: Codeine is a prodrug converted by CYP2D6 to morphine; ultrarapid metabolizers generate toxic morphine levels, the basis of the FDA black box warning in children under 12.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that codeine has an FDA black box warning in children under 12 because codeine is metabolized by CYP2D6 into morphine; children who are ultrarapid metabolizers convert it rapidly, producing dangerously high morphine levels that cause severe respiratory depression and death.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Poor metabolizers would produce too little morphine and inadequate analgesia, not respiratory depression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Codeine is an agonist prodrug, not a brainstem mu-receptor antagonist.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The toxicity is driven by CYP2D6 conversion to morphine, not by reduced renal excretion of codeine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The mechanism is genetic ultrarapid metabolism, not autoinduction by codeine.

questions.stem: A researcher studies a kappa-opioid receptor agonist and observes that it produces a diuretic effect. Which of the following mechanisms best accounts for this kappa-mediated diuresis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inhibition of the release of oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct stimulation of renal tubular sodium reabsorption

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased release of antidiuretic hormone from the pituitary

choices.label: D
choices.text: Activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system

choices.label: E
choices.text: Blockade of aquaporin channels in the collecting duct

explanation.summary: Kappa-opioid receptor activation causes diuresis by inhibiting release of oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone (ADH).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that kappa receptors can cause a prominent diuretic effect by inhibiting the release of oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone (ADH). Less ADH means less water reabsorption and increased urine output.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick attributes the diuresis to reduced ADH/oxytocin release, not direct tubular sodium handling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased ADH release would cause water retention (antidiuresis), the opposite of the observed effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RAAS activation is not the mechanism described for kappa-mediated diuresis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brick describes decreased ADH release, not direct aquaporin blockade.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman with opioid use disorder needs a maintenance opioid that is a full agonist with an ultra-long duration of action to provide a sustained effect. Which of the following medications best fits this description?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Methadone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Codeine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Meperidine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Morphine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tramadol

explanation.summary: Methadone is a full agonist with an ultra-long duration, useful for sustained control in opioid use disorder.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes methadone as a full agonist with an ultra-long duration of action, making it useful for a sustained effect in patients with opioid use disorder. It is listed as a strong, long-duration full agonist.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Codeine is a weak, short-acting full agonist, not an ultra-long-acting maintenance agent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Meperidine is a weak, short-acting full agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Morphine is a strong full agonist but has a short duration of action.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tramadol is a weak, short-acting full agonist.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with cancer-related chronic pain is managed with an opioid delivered by a skin patch that is absorbed slowly, provides stable blood levels, and extends the drug's duration of action even though the opioid itself is short-acting. Which of the following opioids is most commonly used in this way?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fentanyl

choices.label: B
choices.text: Morphine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Buprenorphine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Meperidine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Codeine

explanation.summary: Fentanyl transdermal patches are the most common transdermal opioid; slow skin absorption prolongs duration and gives stable levels for chronic/cancer pain.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that fentanyl transdermal patches are the most common transdermal opioids and are especially useful for cancer-related pain. Although fentanyl is short-acting, the slow rate of absorption through the skin increases its duration of action and provides stable blood levels.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Morphine is a strong short-acting full agonist but is not the opioid identified for transdermal patch use.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist used mainly for opioid use disorder in this brick, not the described cancer-pain patch.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Meperidine is a weak short-acting full agonist and is not used as the transdermal agent described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Codeine is a weak oral antitussive/analgesic prodrug, not the transdermal patch opioid.

questions.stem: A medical student reviews how opioids initiate their intracellular signaling. Opioid receptors, including the mu, kappa, and delta subtypes, belong to which of the following receptor superfamilies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ligand-gated ion channels

choices.label: B
choices.text: G protein-coupled receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Receptor tyrosine kinases

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intracellular nuclear receptors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Voltage-gated ion channels

explanation.summary: Opioid receptors are 7-transmembrane G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that opioid receptors are 7-transmembrane G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) with three primary types: mu, kappa, and delta.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ligand-gated ion channels (e.g., nicotinic, GABA-A) are a different superfamily from the GPCR opioid receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Receptor tyrosine kinases (e.g., insulin receptor) are not the class of opioid receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nuclear receptors are intracellular transcription-factor receptors, unlike the membrane GPCR opioid receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Voltage-gated ion channels respond to membrane potential, not to opioid ligand binding as GPCRs do.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman on chronic opioid therapy for arthritis pain develops persistent constipation that does not improve with continued use. Which of the following best explains this common opioid side effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mu-receptor activation decreases gastrointestinal motility

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kappa-receptor activation increases secretion from intestinal glands

choices.label: C
choices.text: Delta-receptor activation stimulates peristalsis excessively

choices.label: D
choices.text: Opioids block absorption of dietary fiber in the small intestine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Opioids increase release of antidiuretic hormone, drying the stool

explanation.summary: Mu-opioid receptors on enteric neurons reliably decrease GI motility, producing constipation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that mu-opioid receptors are densely distributed in the enteric neurons of the myenteric and submucosal plexuses, and opioid agonists reliably decrease gastric motility, so patients commonly develop constipation and changes in bowel function. Unlike some effects, tolerance to constipation does not readily develop.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick attributes constipation to decreased motility via mu receptors, not increased kappa-mediated intestinal secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Opioids slow rather than stimulate peristalsis; delta receptors are linked to mood effects, not increased gut motility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blocking fiber absorption is not the mechanism of opioid-induced constipation described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ADH release relates to kappa-mediated diuresis, not to the mechanism of opioid constipation.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man brought in after an opioid overdose has a respiratory rate of 4 breaths per minute. His toxicity is due to opioid action at the mu-opioid receptor in the central respiratory centers. Which of the following best describes how opioids depress respiration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They reduce the intrinsic rhythm generators

choices.label: B
choices.text: They paralyze the diaphragm by blocking neuromuscular junction receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: They increase the ventilatory response to rising carbon dioxide

choices.label: D
choices.text: They cause bronchoconstriction that limits gas exchange

choices.label: E
choices.text: They stimulate peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid body

explanation.summary: Opioids depress respiration by reducing the intrinsic rhythm generators in the ventrolateral medulla, slowing the breathing rate.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that opioid agonists depress respiratory activity by causing a reduction to the intrinsic rhythm generators located in the ventrolateral medulla, producing a slower rate of breathing; at toxic doses the respiratory rate may fall to 3-4 breaths per minute.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Opioids act centrally on medullary respiratory centers, not by blocking the neuromuscular junction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Opioids blunt, rather than increase, the ventilatory response to carbon dioxide.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Respiratory depression here is central and rate-based, not due to bronchoconstriction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Opioids depress central respiratory rhythm rather than stimulating carotid body chemoreceptors.

questions.stem: A pharmacology researcher characterizes a selective agonist for the opioid receptor subtype that is expressed in the fewest brain regions. In animal models the compound produces analgesia but is most notable for its antidepressant and anxiolytic effects. Which of the following best describes the basis of these mood effects?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inhibition of oxytocin release from the pituitary

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduction of intrinsic rhythm generators in the medulla

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased motility of the myenteric plexus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Blockade of first-pass hepatic metabolism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Modulation of dopamine signaling

explanation.summary: Delta-opioid receptors, found in the fewest brain areas, produce antidepressant and anxiolytic effects related to dopamine modulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that delta-opioid receptors are found in fewer areas of the brain (caudate, putamen, nucleus accumbens, amygdala) and are primarily involved in mood. In addition to providing analgesia and modulating mu-receptor activity, they produce antidepressant and anxiolytic effects, and the brick attributes these latter effects to dopamine modulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inhibition of oxytocin and ADH release is the mechanism of kappa-mediated diuresis, not delta-mediated mood effects.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reduction of medullary rhythm generators is how mu agonists depress respiration, unrelated to mood effects.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Decreased enteric motility is the mu-receptor mechanism of constipation, not a mood effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: First-pass metabolism is a pharmacokinetic property of the oral route and has nothing to do with receptor-mediated mood effects.

questions.stem: A drug company develops a selective kappa-opioid receptor agonist that produces measurable analgesia in early trials. Despite this, the compound is not pursued as a long-term analgesic. Which of the following adverse effects most likely limited its development?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Severe constipation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Depression and dysphoria

choices.label: C
choices.text: Euphoria and addiction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Suppression of the cough reflex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Excessive sedation

explanation.summary: Kappa-opioid receptors are not targeted for long-term analgesia because their activation produces depression and dysphoria.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that kappa-opioid receptors can provide an analgesic effect and modulate mu-receptor analgesia, but they are typically not targeted for long-term analgesia because they can produce depression and dysphoria (a sense of unease).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Constipation is attributed to mu-opioid receptors densely distributed in enteric neurons, not kappa activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Euphoria, addiction, and physical dependence are consequences of mu-receptor activation, not the reason kappa agonists are avoided.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cough suppression is a clinically useful mu-mediated effect (e.g., codeine), not the limiting kappa adverse effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sedation is described as a CNS effect of potent centrally acting opioids like fentanyl and hydromorphone, not as the kappa-specific problem.

questions.stem: A neuroscientist maps opioid receptor expression in the CNS. She finds one receptor subtype expressed in the hypothalamus and pituitary, where it participates in neuroendocrine regulation and food intake, and notes it is absent from the medulla, pons, and dorsal horn of the spinal cord. Which of the following receptors has this distribution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mu-opioid receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Delta-opioid receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Kappa-opioid receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sigma receptor

explanation.summary: Kappa-opioid receptors are expressed in the hypothalamus and pituitary and have roles in neuroendocrine function and food intake.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes kappa-opioid receptors as widely distributed with prominent roles in diuresis regulation, food intake, pain perception, and neuroendocrine function, and lists the hypothalamus and pituitary among the regions where kappa receptors are found. Figure 2 shows kappa in the hypothalamus and pituitary, whereas the medulla, pons, PAG, and dorsal horn of the spinal cord are labeled as mu.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mu receptors are the subtype shown in the medulla, pons, periaqueductal gray, and dorsal horn of the spinal cord, the regions this receptor is absent from.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Delta receptors are found in the fewest brain areas (caudate, putamen, nucleus accumbens, amygdala) and are tied to mood, not the hypothalamic-pituitary distribution.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nicotinic receptors are not opioid receptors and are not part of the brick's map of opioid receptor expression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sigma is not one of the three primary opioid receptor types described in the brick.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is given a standard analgesic dose of morphine after a hip fracture. Within an hour his respiratory rate drops to 6 breaths per minute. A nurse notes that other patients on the same dose have not had this problem. Which of the following best explains why this patient developed significant respiratory depression?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A concomitant pulmonary condition lowered his threshold for respiratory depression

choices.label: B
choices.text: Morphine is a partial agonist that acts as an antagonist at standard doses

choices.label: C
choices.text: Morphine directly inhibits diaphragmatic contraction in patients with lung disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Standard analgesic doses of morphine routinely produce respiratory depression

choices.label: E
choices.text: Kappa-receptor activation in the pituitary suppresses respiratory drive

explanation.summary: Significant respiratory depression is unlikely at standard analgesic doses unless concomitant factors such as COPD, asthma, hypoxia, or hypercapnia are present.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that mu-opioid receptors are responsible for respiratory depression but that significant respiratory depression is not likely to occur at standard analgesic doses unless other concomitant factors are present, specifically listing asthma, COPD, hypoxia, and hypercapnia. This patient's COPD is the concomitant factor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Morphine is a strong full agonist; buprenorphine is the partial agonist that behaves like an antagonist at high doses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Opioids depress respiration centrally by reducing intrinsic rhythm generators in the ventrolateral medulla, not by direct diaphragm inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick explicitly states that significant respiratory depression is not likely at standard analgesic doses in the absence of concomitant factors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Respiratory depression is a mu-receptor effect in the medulla; kappa receptors in the pituitary relate to neuroendocrine function and diuresis.

questions.stem: A pharmacy student reviewing a table of opioid potencies notices that buprenorphine is the only listed drug whose potency is recorded as 'N/A,' even though its duration is listed as long. Which of the following pharmacologic properties best explains why a potency value is not assigned to buprenorphine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is metabolized by CYP2D6 with highly variable clearance

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is only available as a transdermal patch with slow absorption

choices.label: C
choices.text: At high doses it acts as an antagonist rather than producing a greater effect

choices.label: D
choices.text: It binds mu-opioid receptors with very low affinity

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a prodrug that requires hepatic activation to morphine

explanation.summary: Buprenorphine's potency is not listed because, as a partial agonist, it acts as an antagonist at high doses rather than scaling to a full effect like morphine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation explains that buprenorphine is a partial mu-opioid agonist: at low doses it shows typical agonist effects, but at high doses it acts as an antagonist. This mechanism means it would not be expected to be associated with overdose, and it is the reason the potency for buprenorphine is not listed in Table 1, since potency compares doses against morphine as a full-agonist benchmark.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Variable CYP2D6 metabolism is discussed for codeine and for poor/ultrarapid metabolizers, not as the reason buprenorphine lacks a potency value.
