whyWrongByChoice.B: Fentanyl, not buprenorphine, is the opioid the brick identifies with transdermal patches; route does not remove a drug's potency ranking.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Partial agonists, including buprenorphine, bind the receptor with high affinity; the difference is partial activation, not low affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Codeine is the prodrug converted by CYP2D6 to morphine; buprenorphine is not described as a prodrug.

questions.stem: A hospital pharmacist reviews the opioid orders for a 55-year-old woman who is receiving hydromorphone and oxycodone. To assess her total daily opioid exposure, the pharmacist converts each drug's dose into morphine milligram equivalents (MME). Which of the following best describes what the MME value represents?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The duration of receptor binding for each opioid

choices.label: B
choices.text: The relative dose of each opioid compared to morphine as a standard

choices.label: C
choices.text: The fraction of each opioid that survives first-pass metabolism

choices.label: D
choices.text: The percentage of maximal effect produced at receptor saturation

choices.label: E
choices.text: The number of CYP450 enzymes involved in each opioid's clearance

explanation.summary: Morphine milligram equivalents express an opioid's potency by comparing its relative dose to morphine as the benchmark.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that drug potency describes the amount of drug needed for a given effect, and that with opioid analgesics, morphine is used as the benchmark. For ease, all opioids can be expressed in morphine milligram equivalents (MME), which compares the relative dose of a given opioid to morphine as a standard.

whyWrongByChoice.A: How long receptors remain bound is the definition of duration of action, not MME.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The fraction surviving first-pass metabolism relates to bioavailability of the oral route, not to MME.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Percentage of maximal effect describes efficacy (full vs partial agonist), not potency comparison to morphine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MME is a potency comparison and has nothing to do with the count of metabolizing enzymes.

questions.stem: Two full mu-opioid agonists, Drug X and Drug Y, are compared in a clinical study. Both drugs produce the same maximal degree of analgesia, but Drug X achieves a given level of pain relief at one-tenth the dose required of Drug Y. Which of the following statements best describes Drug X relative to Drug Y?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Drug X has higher efficacy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Drug X has a longer duration of action

choices.label: C
choices.text: Drug X has higher oral bioavailability

choices.label: D
choices.text: Drug X has higher potency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Drug X is a partial agonist

explanation.summary: Potency describes the amount of drug needed for a given effect; a drug that achieves the same effect at a lower dose is more potent.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines drug potency as the amount of drug needed for a given effect, and notes that opioids are often described as weak or strong in potency. Since Drug X needs one-tenth the dose of Drug Y for the same analgesic effect, it is the more potent drug.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both are full agonists producing the same maximal effect, so their efficacy is the same; efficacy concerns the size of the maximal response, not the dose needed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Duration of action refers to how long receptors remain bound, which is not addressed by comparing doses needed for an effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bioavailability is a route-dependent pharmacokinetic property; the comparison here is about dose needed for effect, not absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A partial agonist produces a lesser maximal effect than a full agonist; Drug X reaches the same maximal analgesia, so it is not a partial agonist.

questions.stem: A pharmacology professor explains that one property of an opioid agonist determines whether it is better suited for acute pain versus chronic pain management, and that this property can be altered by the dosage form in which the drug is given. Which of the following best defines this property?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The amount of drug needed to produce a given effect

choices.label: B
choices.text: The percentage of maximal effect the drug can produce

choices.label: C
choices.text: The strength of the drug's binding to the receptor

choices.label: D
choices.text: The proportion of drug that reaches the systemic circulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: The length of time the receptors remain bound by the drug

explanation.summary: Duration of action is how long receptors remain bound, and it determines whether an opioid is used for acute (short-acting) or chronic (long-acting) pain.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines the duration of action of an opioid agonist as how long the receptors remain bound, or practically, how long the medication will exert its effects. It notes that how the drug is given (the dosage form) can play a role in duration, and that short-acting opioids are used for acute pain while long-acting opioids are used for chronic pain management.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The amount of drug needed for a given effect defines potency, not the property that sorts acute from chronic use.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Percentage of maximal effect defines efficacy, distinguishing full from partial agonists.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Binding affinity is shared by both full and partial agonists and is not what the dosage form alters.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The proportion reaching systemic circulation is bioavailability, a route-dependent property rather than the acute-versus-chronic determinant.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with chronic severe pain from metastatic disease has been managed with short-acting morphine but needs a long-acting agent. Her physician wants a strong full agonist with a long duration of action and does not want to use an agent primarily associated with opioid use disorder treatment. Which of the following opioids best fits these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oxymorphone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydromorphone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Meperidine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxycodone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tramadol

explanation.summary: Oxymorphone is a strong, long-duration full agonist, making it suited to chronic pain management.
explanation.whyCorrect: Table 1 in the brick lists oxymorphone as a full agonist with strong potency and long duration. The brick states that long-acting opioids are used for chronic pain management. Methadone is the other strong long-duration full agonist, but it is the agent the brick highlights for sustained effect in opioid use disorder, which the physician wishes to avoid.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hydromorphone is a strong full agonist but has a short duration of action per Table 1.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Meperidine is listed as a weak, short-duration full agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxycodone is listed with a short duration of action in Table 1.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tramadol is a weak full agonist with a short duration of action.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with moderate pain after a dental procedure is prescribed an oral opioid. His clinician deliberately selects an agent classified as a weak full agonist rather than a strong one. Which of the following opioids was most likely prescribed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fentanyl

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oxymorphone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tramadol

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hydromorphone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Morphine

explanation.summary: Tramadol is a weak-potency, short-duration full agonist; codeine and meperidine are the other weak agonists in Table 1.
explanation.whyCorrect: Table 1 in the brick classifies tramadol as a full agonist with weak potency and short duration. The other weak full agonists listed are codeine and meperidine. Potency is expressed relative to morphine as the benchmark and described as weak or strong.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fentanyl is a strong full agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Oxymorphone is a strong full agonist with a long duration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hydromorphone is a strong full agonist, described as very potent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Morphine is a strong full agonist and serves as the potency benchmark.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a persistent dry cough after a viral illness is prescribed a codeine-containing syrup. Which of the following best describes the site at which codeine exerts its antitussive effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enteric neurons of the submucosal plexus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cough center within the medulla

choices.label: C
choices.text: Kappa receptors in the pituitary

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dorsal horn of the spinal cord

choices.label: E
choices.text: Delta receptors in the nucleus accumbens

explanation.summary: Codeine suppresses cough by depressing the cough reflex within the cough center of the medulla.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that codeine is frequently used for cough suppression, which is achieved as opioid agonists depress the cough reflex within the cough center of the medulla. Cough suppression is listed alongside analgesia and sedation as a clinical use of opioids.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enteric neuron mu receptors mediate decreased GI motility and constipation, not cough suppression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Kappa receptors in the pituitary relate to neuroendocrine function and diuresis regulation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The dorsal horn is a mu-receptor site related to pain transmission, not the cough reflex.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Delta receptors in the nucleus accumbens are involved in mood, not cough.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man is intubated in the intensive care unit for acute respiratory failure. Immediately after endotracheal intubation, the team starts a continuous infusion of fentanyl. Which of the following best describes the primary goal of this medication strategy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To suppress the cough reflex in the medulla

choices.label: B
choices.text: To increase gastric motility during enteral feeding

choices.label: C
choices.text: To produce diuresis by inhibiting ADH release

choices.label: D
choices.text: To avoid first-pass metabolism of the drug

choices.label: E
choices.text: To provide analgesia and sedation for ventilator compliance

explanation.summary: Continuous fentanyl infusions after intubation target analgosedation, maintaining patient comfort and compliance with mechanical ventilation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation notes that very potent opioids like fentanyl and hydromorphone produce strong sedation through CNS actions. Although this side effect is concerning in outpatients, it is often targeted in inpatients: continuous infusions (drips) of fentanyl are frequently used immediately after endotracheal intubation to target analgesia and sedation, or analgosedation, which maintains patient comfort and compliance with mechanical ventilation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cough suppression is the clinical use described for codeine, not the goal of a post-intubation fentanyl drip.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Opioids reliably decrease, not increase, gastric motility.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Diuresis via inhibited ADH release is a kappa-receptor effect, not a treatment goal here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Although IV infusion does avoid first-pass metabolism, that is a pharmacokinetic feature of the route, not the clinical purpose of the infusion.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man is seen in clinic for follow-up of chronic severe pain after back surgery. He is ambulatory, eating normally, and wants a convenient regimen he can manage at home so he can return to golfing. Which of the following routes of opioid administration is most appropriate for him?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oral

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intravenous

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intramuscular

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intrathecal

choices.label: E
choices.text: Subcutaneous infusion

explanation.summary: The oral route is convenient, non-invasive, and best for mild, moderate, and chronic pain, making it the appropriate outpatient choice.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that many common opioids are available orally and that this route is best for mild, moderate, and chronic pain because it is convenient and non-invasive for patients. In the brick's case, a PO medication is described as likely sufficient to control the patient's chronic pain after back surgery.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IV is the preferred route for acute severe pain with rapid onset, not for convenient chronic outpatient management.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IM is the least common opioid route, reserved for acute situations where IV access is not yet obtained.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intrathecal administration is not among the routes the brick describes for routine chronic pain management.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Subcutaneous infusion is not a route the brick presents as the convenient outpatient option for chronic pain.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man arrives at a rural emergency department with an open femur fracture and severe pain. The nurse has been unable to establish intravenous access after multiple attempts. The physician wants to give an opioid now that avoids first-pass metabolism. Which of the following routes is most appropriate in this situation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oral

choices.label: B
choices.text: Transdermal patch

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rectal

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intramuscular

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sublingual

explanation.summary: The intramuscular route avoids first-pass metabolism and is helpful in acute situations where IV access has not been obtained.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes IM as the least common route for opioids but one that can be helpful in acute situations where IV access is not yet obtained or possible. First-pass metabolism is avoided with this route, although onset is slower than IV, and bioavailability is generally good though not as high as IV.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The oral route subjects the drug to first-pass metabolism by the liver and is suited to mild, moderate, or chronic pain rather than acute severe pain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Transdermal absorption is slow and is used for chronic or sustained pain, not for immediate relief of acute severe pain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The rectal route is not one the brick describes for acute severe pain when IV access fails.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sublingual administration is not among the routes the brick presents for acute severe pain management.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman on a stable dose of oxycodone for chronic pain is started on a new antifungal that is a strong inhibitor of CYP3A4. One week later she is markedly drowsy, has not had a bowel movement in five days, and her respiratory rate is 9 breaths per minute. Which of the following best explains her new symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The antifungal induced CYP3A4, accelerating opioid clearance

choices.label: B
choices.text: The antifungal converted oxycodone into a partial agonist

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of CYP3A4 raised her opioid levels and enhanced the side effect profile

choices.label: D
choices.text: The antifungal blocked opioid absorption from the GI tract

choices.label: E
choices.text: The antifungal displaced oxycodone from mu receptors, causing withdrawal

explanation.summary: CYP450 inhibitors increase opioid levels, enhancing side effects such as respiratory depression, sedation, and constipation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that many opioids are metabolized by CYP3A4 and CYP2D6, creating hundreds of potential drug-drug interactions. Medications that inhibit or induce the CYP450 system can increase or decrease opioid levels, and altered levels can enhance the side effect profile (respiratory depression, sedation, constipation). A CYP3A4 inhibitor would raise oxycodone levels, explaining her drowsiness, constipation, and slowed breathing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An inducer would decrease opioid levels and reduce effects; an inhibitor does the opposite.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Enzyme inhibition alters drug levels; it does not change a full agonist into a partial agonist.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blocked absorption would lower opioid exposure and lessen, not enhance, these effects.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Withdrawal would not present as sedation, constipation, and respiratory depression, which are signs of excess opioid effect.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with chronic pain well controlled on an oral opioid metabolized by CYP3A4 is started on a medication known to induce the CYP450 system. Two weeks later he reports that his pain has returned and that each dose seems to wear off sooner. Which of the following best explains this change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Development of a CYP2D6 poor metabolizer phenotype

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased opioid metabolism lowering plasma opioid levels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Conversion of the opioid to a kappa-selective metabolite

choices.label: D
choices.text: Upregulation of first-pass metabolism restricted to the GI tract

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased opioid bioavailability producing receptor desensitization

explanation.summary: CYP450 inducers decrease opioid levels, reducing analgesic effect.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick emphasizes awareness of medications that inhibit or induce the CYP450 system because they have the potential to increase or decrease opioid levels. Opioids metabolized by CYP3A4 and 2D6 can have significant drug-drug interactions. An inducer speeds metabolism, lowering opioid levels and shortening the effect, which explains the return of pain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A poor metabolizer phenotype is a genetic polymorphism that prolongs duration, not something acquired from a drug, and it would increase rather than decrease opioid effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick does not describe induction producing kappa-selective metabolites; the interaction is about changing opioid levels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Induction of CYP450 is a hepatic enzyme effect on overall metabolism, not an effect confined to the GI tract.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Increased bioavailability would raise opioid levels and enhance effects, the opposite of what occurred.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman of Middle Eastern descent is prescribed a standard oral opioid regimen after abdominal surgery. She reports that each dose relieves her pain for a much shorter time than expected, and she is asking for doses more frequently than scheduled. Which of the following best explains her response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She is a CYP2D6 poor metabolizer with reduced drug clearance

choices.label: B
choices.text: She has developed tolerance from prior chronic opioid use

choices.label: C
choices.text: She is an intermediate metabolizer with slightly prolonged drug action

choices.label: D
choices.text: The oral route has bypassed first-pass metabolism in her case

choices.label: E
choices.text: She is a CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizer who clears the drug very quickly

explanation.summary: Ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizers clear opioids very quickly and experience significantly shorter durations of action; this phenotype is common in individuals of Middle Eastern and North African descent.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that a single nucleotide polymorphism in the 2D6 enzyme can make an individual an ultrarapid (UR), normal, intermediate, or poor metabolizer. A UR metabolizer clears medication from the body very quickly and experiences significantly shorter durations of action with opioids. The UR polymorphism can be common in individuals of Middle Eastern and North African descent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Poor metabolizers have prolonged, not shortened, duration of action and are most common among individuals of Asian descent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nothing in the vignette indicates prior chronic opioid use, and the brick attributes ethnically varied responses to altered pharmacogenomics.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An intermediate metabolizer would not show the markedly shortened duration described; the brick ties short duration to the ultrarapid phenotype.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oral drugs are always subject to first-pass metabolism; bypassing it would raise, not shorten, drug effect.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man of Asian descent is taking an oral opioid for chronic pain after back surgery. His pain is controlled, but each dose leaves him too sleepy to do anything for many hours. His physician suspects he is a CYP2D6 poor metabolizer. Which of the following is the most appropriate adjustment to his regimen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Extend the interval between doses or lower the dose

choices.label: B
choices.text: Switch to intravenous administration of the same opioid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add a CYP2D6 inhibitor to stabilize drug levels

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increase the dose to overcome the sedation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Switch to a transdermal fentanyl patch at an equivalent dose

explanation.summary: In a suspected poor metabolizer with enhanced side effects, extending the time between doses or lowering the dose decreases side effects while still providing pain relief.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's case resolution states that because the patient is of Asian descent there is a strong possibility he is a poor metabolizer experiencing enhanced side effects. It recommends considering extending the time between doses or lowering the dose to decrease the side effects while still providing pain relief, since a single dose in a poor metabolizer can last two to three times as long as expected.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick notes a PO medication will likely be sufficient for his chronic pain; IV is for acute severe pain and would not address prolonged drug action.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A CYP inhibitor would further increase opioid levels and worsen sedation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increasing the dose would intensify the excessive sedation caused by slowed clearance and could lead to unintended overdose.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transdermal fentanyl is described for cancer-related and sustained pain; it does not correct the problem of prolonged drug action in a poor metabolizer.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man who has been using prescription opioids recreationally describes intense euphoria with each dose and now experiences distressing symptoms whenever he tries to stop. Activation of which of the following receptors best accounts for the euphoria and physical dependence he describes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Kappa-opioid receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Delta-opioid receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sigma receptor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mu-opioid receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Omega receptor

explanation.summary: Mu-opioid receptor activation affects mood and reward pathways, leading to euphoria, physical dependence, and addiction.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that mu-opioid receptors are found in regions involved with sensory and affective components of pain and modulation of many other behaviors, including reward pathways. When activated, these receptors affect mood and rewarding behavior, so activation of mu receptors can lead to physical dependence, addiction, depression, and euphoria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Kappa activation produces dysphoria and depression, not euphoria and dependence.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Delta receptors are tied to mood via antidepressant and anxiolytic effects, not the reward-driven euphoria and dependence described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sigma is not one of the three primary opioid receptors in the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Omega is not an opioid receptor type.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man receives intravenous morphine for severe pain from a kidney stone and reports marked relief within minutes. Activation of mu-opioid receptors in which of the following regions produces downstream effects that block the perception of pain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nucleus accumbens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hippocampus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Periaqueductal gray

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pituitary

choices.label: E
choices.text: Myenteric plexus

explanation.summary: Mu-receptor activation in the periaqueductal gray (PAG) produces downstream effects that block the perception of pain.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that opioids achieve analgesia because activation of mu-opioid receptors in the PAG produces downstream effects that block the perception of pain. As mu receptors in the PAG are activated, downstream effects provide sensory input to higher centers in the brain and block the sensation of pain.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The nucleus accumbens expresses mu, kappa, and delta receptors and is tied to reward and mood, not the PAG-mediated pain block.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The hippocampus expresses mu and kappa receptors but is not the region the brick identifies for the analgesic pain block.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The pituitary is a kappa-receptor site related to neuroendocrine function and ADH/oxytocin release.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mu receptors in the enteric plexuses decrease GI motility, producing constipation rather than analgesia.

questions.stem: A neuroanatomy student studies a map of opioid receptor distribution in the CNS. She notes that caudate, putamen, amygdala, and nucleus accumbens each express all three primary opioid receptor subtypes. Which of the following regions expresses mu and kappa receptors but lacks delta receptors?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Caudate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Amygdala

choices.label: C
choices.text: Putamen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nucleus accumbens

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thalamus

explanation.summary: Delta receptors are found in the fewest brain areas; the thalamus and hippocampus express mu and kappa but not delta.
explanation.whyCorrect: Figure 1 in the brick maps the three primary opioid receptor types: the thalamus and hippocampus are labeled with mu and kappa only, while the caudate, putamen, amygdala, and nucleus accumbens carry mu, kappa, and delta. The brick states that delta-opioid receptors are found in fewer areas of the brain, primarily the caudate, putamen, nucleus accumbens, and amygdala, which are involved in mood.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The caudate is one of the regions listed as expressing delta receptors along with mu and kappa.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The amygdala expresses all three receptor types, including delta.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The putamen is listed among the delta-expressing regions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The nucleus accumbens expresses mu, kappa, and delta receptors.

questions.stem: A pharmacology student examines a dose-response graph of two opioids acting at the mu receptor. Drug 1 reaches 100% of maximal effect at high doses. Drug 2 rises in parallel with Drug 1 at low doses but plateaus at roughly 60% of maximal effect no matter how much the dose is increased. Which of the following best describes Drug 2?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A full agonist with lower potency than Drug 1

choices.label: B
choices.text: A partial agonist that acts like a normal agonist at low doses

choices.label: C
choices.text: A full agonist with a shorter duration of action

choices.label: D
choices.text: A competitive antagonist with no intrinsic activity

choices.label: E
choices.text: A full agonist that is a CYP2D6 prodrug

explanation.summary: A partial agonist acts like a normal agonist at low doses but produces a lesser maximal effect than a full agonist at high doses.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that a partial agonist binds a receptor with high affinity but only induces partial activation: at low doses these drugs act like normal agonists, but at high doses there is a lesser effect than with full agonists. Figure 1 shows the partial agonist curve plateauing at a lower percent of maximum effect, illustrating its lower efficacy compared with the full agonist's 100%.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A less potent full agonist would still reach 100% maximal effect at a higher dose; a lower plateau reflects lower efficacy, not lower potency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Duration of action describes how long receptors stay bound and is not shown by a plateau in maximal effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An antagonist produces no agonist effect at all; Drug 2 clearly produces a substantial effect at low doses.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Being a prodrug (like codeine) does not cap the maximal effect; once converted, the active drug would still be a full agonist.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman with a severe burn injury requires a strong opioid for acute pain that will be given intravenously in short intervals. The physician wants a full agonist with strong potency and a short duration of action that is not codeine and not morphine. Which of the following opioids best fits these criteria?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydromorphone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Methadone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Buprenorphine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Meperidine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oxymorphone

explanation.summary: Hydromorphone is a strong, short-acting full agonist suited to acute pain.
explanation.whyCorrect: Table 1 in the brick lists hydromorphone as a full agonist with strong potency and short duration. The brick states that short-acting opioids are used for acute pain and describes hydromorphone (with fentanyl) as a very potent opioid capable of strong CNS effects.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Methadone is a strong full agonist but has a long (ultra-long) duration of action.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist with a long duration and no listed potency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Meperidine is a full agonist with short duration but weak, not strong, potency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxymorphone is strong and full but has a long duration, better suited to chronic pain.

questions.stem: A clinical pharmacist counsels a hospital team on pharmacogenomic variability in opioid response. She notes that the ultrarapid CYP2D6 metabolizer polymorphism, which shortens opioid duration of action, is common among individuals of Middle Eastern and North African descent. According to the prevalence the team is taught, up to approximately what proportion of these individuals may carry this polymorphism?

explanation.summary: The ultrarapid CYP2D6 polymorphism can be present in up to 30% of individuals of Middle Eastern and North African descent.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the ultrarapid (UR) polymorphism can be common, up to 30%, in individuals of Middle Eastern and North African descent, and that UR metabolizers clear medication very quickly with significantly shorter durations of opioid action. By comparison, poor metabolizers are most common among individuals of Asian descent, at up to 35%.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 5% understates the prevalence the brick gives for the UR polymorphism in these populations.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 10% is well below the up-to-30% figure the brick states.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 20% is lower than the brick's stated ceiling of 30%.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 50% overstates the prevalence; the brick gives up to 30% for UR metabolizers (and up to 35% for poor metabolizers in Asian populations).
